source.title: Fourier Circuits in Neural Networks and Transformers: A Case Study of Modular Arithmetic with Multiple Inputs
source.authors: Chenyang Li; Yingyu Liang; Zhenmei Shi; Zhao Song; Tianyi Zhou

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper follows the original grokking experimental protocol on modular-addition tasks, using training and validation accuracy over training steps, while varying the number of inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking on all tested k settings and says it weakens as k increases. The settings use roughly equal dataset sizes and 50% training data, so they do not test whether a smaller training set takes more optimization. The Fourier analyses report endpoint representations, not gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, or progress measures over time.
record.test_reason: Section 5.3 follows the original grokking protocol from arXiv:2201.02177. It trains small transformers on modular addition with k = 2, 3, 4 and 5 inputs, 50% training data and AdamW with weight decay. It reports training and validation accuracy over steps (Figure 4), which bears directly on V1. The rest of the paper is max-margin theory plus endpoint Fourier analyses, which test no version directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusion is theoretical: max-margin one-hidden-layer networks with at least 2^(2k-2)(p-1) neurons learn single-frequency Fourier features covering all frequencies, and experiments on MLPs and one-layer transformers agree. On grokking, they report it for every k with weakening as k grows. They attribute this to task complexity and an NTK-to-feature-learning transition, and admit their theorem cannot fully explain Figure 4.
record.recipe_differences: The paper says it follows the original experimental protocol, but studies modular addition with k = 2, 3, 4, and 5 inputs and uses different p values to keep dataset sizes roughly equal.
record.method_sensitivity: Grokking strength varies with k: the authors state that it weakens as k increases. The experiments vary p to keep dataset sizes roughly equal and use 50% of the data for training.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD-trained one-hidden-layer polynomial networks (k = 3, 4, 5) end with single-frequency Fourier neurons covering all frequencies. One-layer transformers show 2-D cosine-shaped W_KQ attention matrices. This matches max-margin theory but is shown only at endpoints, with no comparison across seeds or hyperparameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under margin maximization, networks learning k-input modular addition converge to a Fourier-feature solution, with each neuron tied to one frequency and every frequency covered.

record.code_released: The authors state that code is provided in supplemental material; no URL for that material is stated. The paper identifies https://github.com/Sea-Snell/grokking as the open-source repository on which their code is based.
record.problems: The grokking curves are shown as figures without numerical accuracy or step values in the text. The reported comparison varies k rather than training-set size, and the experiments use 50% of the data for training. Results were run three times and Figure 4 reports a mean and variance range, but the numerical range is not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks: the training fraction is fixed at 50% and dataset sizes are held roughly equal. No numeric step counts or accuracies are given; results are figure-only.
The lazy-to-rich (NTK to feature learning) account is invoked only as an interpretation. Initialization scale and weight norm are not varied, and no non-algorithmic data are used.
Weight decay is fixed (1e-3); no critical dataset size or ungrokking is studied.
There are no progress measures over training time; the Fourier analyses are endpoint only.
Only AdamW is used, with no control of optimizer or numerical choices.

missing.what: Endpoint Fourier-sparsity results: maximum normalized power near 1 for all neurons, and a near-uniform frequency distribution versus random initialization. These cover MLPs (k = 3, 4, 5) and one-layer transformer attention matrices (k = 3, 4, 5). They are relevant context for V6-type comparisons of which algorithm networks learn.

record.verdict_notes: The explanation in Section 5.3 is internally muddled: it says harder tasks need more steps to fit, yet grokking weakens. The grokking-strength metric (steps to regime switch) is described but never quantified. Results come from 3 seeds with a mean and variance band, figure only. The model depth is inconsistent between Section 5.3 and Appendix H.1. Tranche could arguably be T3, since the protocol is the original but the task is a k-input variant.

versions.untested_parts: The relation between training-set size and optimization delay; the experiments use 50% training data and vary k, choosing different p values to keep dataset sizes roughly equal.
